newsitem.title: UK: METALS OUTLOOK -- MARKETS FOCUS ON TIGHTNESS.
newsitem.headline: METALS OUTLOOK -- MARKETS FOCUS ON TIGHTNESS.

text.p: The metals market this week will focus on tightness in aluminium and zinc after more scorching gains and a warning by the London Metal Exchange (LME) last week.
Technical tightness in aluminium squeezed three month prices to a fresh 22-month peak of $1,775 per tonne last Thursday.
This was a gain of $213 or nearly 14 percent since July 16.
The market eased in a correction the following day and ended the week at $1,746, but the market had a strong underpinning, analysts said.
The rise was kicked off by a stand-off between short options grantors and longs who tightly held the important dates, analysts said. Banks, investment funds and other speculators fuelled the rise.
Prices found good support around $1,730/33 on Friday and may consolidate above $1,700 ahead of another push higher, analysts said.
An upward bias should be seen in the run-up to next week's "Third Wednesday" pricing for the August date, where the first lump of tightness resides.
"The only thing that will hit prices is if tightness in August disappears and tightness usually gets worse before it gets better," said analyst Robin Bahr of broker Brandeis.
With further tightness centred around November, the cash/threes spread flared out to a $20 backwardation on Thursday, ending the week at $15/$20.
The market will watch closely the aftermath of a warning by the LME regarding members who "exercise a dominant position in the market".

LME Chief Executive David King, underlining the exchange's rules, said in a notice last week that even if such a member had no "untoward intent", great caution must be taken. Using a dominant position to make certain market users pay more than they would otherwise had to pay was improper.
Causing greatest concern to the LME is extreme tightness in very nearby spreads such as cash/day and tomorrow/next day, analysts said.
For the moment these spreads are not in backwardation, but eyes will be on aluminium as the August date approaches, they added.
The market will be watching producer stocks data from the International Primary Aluminium Institute, due to be released at 1000 GMT on Monday.
"We would expect to see a small rise here in unwrought stocks," said analyst Larry Kaplan of Flemings Global Mining Group.

"In May there were still close to long-term historical lows, partly as a result of strong first half 1997 demand and partly on companies' improved inventory and logistics management," he added in a commentary.
Zinc is another metal which has been squeezed, with a cash/threes backwardation that zoomed up to $155 late on Friday from $100 for most of the previous two weeks.
Now that the market has let off steam in a violent correction on July 29, prices have a more solid base to continue to move higher as the September tight dates approach, analysts said.

But the three months market has regained 61 percent of its $305 plunge, a key retracement level, and may take a pause. Some players believe the focus will move to the cash market, which was bid up on Friday.
Many market players believe that Chinese smelters which sold more metal than they could produce are covering some of their short positions but also rolling over a substantial number.
This sparked interest in October dates last week, pushing out the October/threes spread to a $65 backwardation.
The Chinese are also taking advantage of high prices to sell forward, traders said.
Copper is the third metal with a backwardation in the benchmark cash/threes spread. It narrowed sharply after two weeks of tight dates passed last month and stabilised around $30 last week.
Prices surged to a high of $2,335 on Thursday, helped by a lower than normal stocks rise and rallies in other metals.
But it quickly sank back below $2,330 on Friday as stocks rose by 2,925 tonnes, reminding players of the summer slowdown and what many regard as a looming surplus. It ended the week at $2,288.
